title: Introduction to Philosophy: Global Philosophies
description: Introduction to African, indigenous American, Asian, European, and Hispanic philosophies. Exploration of how diverse philosophies across the globe help address crises like climate change, social injustice, and military conflicts or are reflected in social, economic, and political institutions.

title: Introduction to Philosophy: Ethics
description: Philosophical inquiry, with emphasis on problems of moral value. Students are encouraged to think independently and formulate their own tentative conclusions concerning a variety of vital contemporary issues facing individuals and society.

title: Introduction to Philosophy: Knowledge and Reality
description: Introduction to philosophical inquiry with emphasis on problems of knowledge and reality. Students are encouraged to think independently and formulate their own tentative conclusions.

title: Introduction to Logic
description: Introduction to deductive and inductive logic. Logic and language. Analysis of fallacies. Uses of logic in science and in daily life.

title: Technology and Human Nature
description: Interaction of technology and human nature. Environmental problems associated with rapid development of technology. Responses to problems by various philosophers and writers.

title: Critical Thinking and Composition
description: Introduction to critical thinking and writing. Evaluation and development of correct reasoning and effective style and organization in argumentative writing. Correct deductive and inductive reasoning. Fallacies. Critical appraisal of evidence. Construction of rebuttals and counter-arguments.

title: Experimental Topics
description: Selected topics.

title: Special Study
description: Individual study.

title: Philosophy and Human Nature
description: Concept of human nature. Descriptive and normative aspects of major theories of human nature.

title: Women and Philosophy
description: Exploration of women’s contributions to philosophy, both present and historically. Concepts relating to women and femininity, both by the philosophical canon and by more recent feminist philosophers.

title: Philosophy and Literature
description: Study of literature of philosophical significance and of philosophical problems of literature.

title: A Major Philosophical Topic
description: General introduction to a major philosophical topic (e.g. cosmopolitan justice, freedom of the will, the nature and existence of God, theory and evidence).

title: Philosophy, Racism, and Justice
description: Philosophical concepts and theories of racism and racial justice. Arguments for and against such theories.

title: Social Ethics
description: Ethical issues of contemporary life. Individualism vs. collectivism; democracy vs. dictatorship; ethical problems arising in law, medicine, business, government and interpersonal relationships.

title: Biomedical Ethics
description: Value judgments upon which medicine is based and the ethical issues which medicine faces.

title: Environmental Ethics
description: Development of traditional values concerning the natural environment. Reasons for altering values in light of modern changes in relationship of human beings to the environment. Application of ethical principles to actions affecting the environment.

title: Ethics-Food
description: Ethics of what we eat to include fair-trade food sourcing, food rituals, shaming, waste; use of GMOs, veganism, and vegetarianism.

title: Philosophy of Business Ethics
description: Moral status of business practices; arguments and theories regarding ways to run businesses and corporations; issues that arise in everyday practices of businesses.
notes: May not be taken in place of

title: Philosophy and the Internet
description: Investigate questions raised by the development of internet-driven culture; supply the conceptual tools necessary to make critical value judgments about the internet and society; and develop a practice of approaching the internet with philosophically rigorous inquiry.

title: Ethics and Artificial Intelligence
description: Discussion of ethics and artificial intelligence (AI). May include ethical investigation of biases, preferences, and information of users and technology. Students research, investigate, and discuss ethical implications of AI and its impacts on society.
notes: For this course to count as fulfilling the GE requirement for Explorations, students must have 60 or more units by the time they complete this course.

title: AI and the Public Good
description: Exploration of ethical and political challenges posed by artificial intelligence. Students analyze theoretical texts, practical policies, and real-world cases to assess AI’s impact on society and develop informed, ethical responses to emerging technologies.

title: Philosophy and Video Games
description: Metaphysical and ethical investigations into experience playing video games. Topics may include how video games are similar or different from reality, whether we have free will when playing a video game, and what is ethically permissible in a video game.

title: Morality of War and Peace
description: Historical and contemporary arguments regarding morality of war, pacifism, and terrorism, with contemporary applications.

title: Logic and the Law
description: Logic in legal contexts. Inductive reasoning methods applied to legal briefs, case studies, and LSATs. Construction, presentation, and evaluation of written and oral arguments, using historical and contemporary legal decisions.

title: Morality and the Law
description: Understanding and application of the law via contemporary moral controversies in case law and legal practice.

title: Ethics Bowl
description: Interdisciplinary, case-study approach to contemporary ethical issues. Creative, critical thinking skills and theoretical ethical frameworks;

title: Global Justice
description: Current debates in political philosophy concerning the justification, content, and scope of duties of global justice to include distributive justice, nationalism vs. cosmopolitanism, morality of immigration controls, justification of human rights, and limits of sovereignty.

title: Chinese Philosophy
description: Philosophical traditions which have shaped the intellectual life and culture of China. Emphasis on foundational texts surviving from pre-Han China.

title: Buddhist Philosophy
description: Intellectual traditions within Buddhism, both ancient and contemporary, including key areas of metaphysics, epistemology, and axiology.

title: History of Philosophy: Pre-Socratic through Medieval
description: From Pre-Socratic through Medieval.
notes: Not open to students with credit in Philosophy 411 and 412.

title: History of Philosophy: Renaissance and Early Modern
description: Renaissance and early modern philosophy.
notes: Not open to students with credit in Philosophy 412 and 413.

title: Experimental Topics
description: Selected topics.

title: Special Study
description: Individual study.

title: Nineteenth-Century European Philosophy
description: Major European philosophers of the nineteenth century. May include Hegel, Kierkegaard, Marx, Mill, Nietzsche, and Schopenhauer.

title: Twentieth-Century Continental Philosophy
description: Major figures and movements in European philosophy from Husserl to the present.

title: Existentialism
description: The philosophical aspects of existentialism. Major emphasis is on the diversity of thought within a common approach as this is shown in individual thinkers.

title: Theory of Ethics
description: Advanced topics in ethical theory, including normative ethics and meta-ethics. May include historical or contemporary readings or both. Issues may include content of moral value, nature of moral judgment, and accounts of virtue and right action.

title: Philosophy of Law
description: Philosophical and ethical investigation into the nature of law, rights, liberty, responsibility, and punishment.

title: Political Philosophy
description: Selected aspects of the political structures within which we live, such as law, power, sovereignty, justice, liberty, welfare.

title: Philosophy of Art
description: The nature of aesthetic experience. Principal Western theories of art in relation to actual artistic production and to the function of art in society.

title: Global Aesthetics
description: How cultures beyond Amero-Eurocentric traditions developed aesthetic theories complementing, challenging, or expanding more often taught theories. Historical and contemporary works representing a spectrum of philosophies around the globe.

title: Deductive Logic
description: Principles of inference for symbolic deductive systems; connectives, quantifiers, relations and sets. Interpretations of deductive systems in mathematics, science and ordinary language.
notes: Not open to students with credit in

title: Theory of Knowledge
description: Philosophical analysis of knowledge, including conceptions of belief, justification, and truth.

title: Metaphysics
description: Prominent theories of reality, e.g., realism and nominalism, materialism and idealism, teleology and determinism.

title: Philosophy of Language
description: An introduction to theories of meaning for natural languages and formal systems; concepts of truth, synonymy and analyticity; related epistemological and ontological problems.

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: Philosophical analysis of the nature and existence of God.

title: Philosophy of Mind
description: Prominent theories and arguments regarding relation between mind and body. Varieties of dualism considered along with major materialist rivals.

title: Philosophy of Science
description: The basic concepts and methods underlying contemporary scientific thought. Contributions of the special sciences to a view of the universe as a whole.

title: Queer Theory
description: Philosophical aspects of queer theory. Sexualized identity intersections with ability, nationality, race, and other categories. Desire, gender, sex, sexuality; affect, embodiment, identity, and temporality.

title: Empirical Perspectives of Buddhism
description: Historical and contemporary Buddhist scholarship and practice.

title: Asian Philosophies
description: Dimensions of Asian philosophies, past and present. Encounter between Buddhism and post-modern science, contemporary Asian philosophers (“global gurus”) and their impact on non-Asian cultures, enigmatic notion of emptiness (sunya, wu).

title: A Major Philosopher
description: The writings of one major philosopher.

title: A Major Philosophical Tradition
description: Focused study of a major philosophical tradition (e.g., Platonism, Confucianism, positivism).

title: A Major Philosophical Problem
description: Focused study of a major philosophical problem (e.g., the problem of evil, the problem of other minds, the existence of God).

title: Philosophical Methods
description: Focused study of major philosophical methods (e.g., uncertain inferences and non-bivalent logics, phenomenological method, deconstruction).

title: Selected Topics
description: A critical analysis of a major problem or movement in philosophy.

title: Special Study
description: Directed individual study in philosophy on a theme or topic chosen in consultation with the instructor.

title: Seminar in the History of Philosophy
description: A major philosopher, school, or problem. Their historical roots and subsequent historical significance.

title: Seminar in Philosophical Problems: Values
description: Problems in such fields as ethics, politics, aesthetics.

title: Seminar in Philosophical Problems: Knowledge and Reality
description: A problem or group of problems in metaphysics, epistemology and logic.

title: Seminar in Current Philosophical Issues
description: Problems in current philosophical publications.

title: Seminar in Teaching Philosophy
description: Critical thinking and writing skills to teach philosophy. Syllabus construction, teaching techniques, assessment, and outcomes measurement.

title: Seminar in Selected Topics
description: Intensive study in specific areas of philosophy.

title: Studies in Philosophy
description: Preparation for the comprehensive examination for students taking the M.A. (non-thesis option). Maximum credit three units applicable to a master’s degree. Offered Credit/No Credit only.

title: Special Study
description: Individual study.

title: Thesis
description: Preparation of a project or thesis for the master’s degree.

title: Thesis Extension
description: Registration required in any semester or term following assignment of RP in Course 799A in which the student expects to use the facilities and resources of the university; also student must be registered in the course when the completed thesis is granted final approval.

title: Comprehensive Examination Extension
description: Registration required of students whose only requirement is completion of the comprehensive examination for the master’s degree. Registration in 799C limited to two semesters.
